content: In the physical sciences, an intensive property, also referred to as a bulk property, is a physical characteristic of a system that remains independent of the system's size or the quantity of material present within it. Conversely, an extensive property is one that depends on the size of the system or the amount of material it contains. Examples of extensive properties include mass, volume, and energy, as these values scale with the quantity of the substance. For instance, density is an intensive property because it is a ratio of mass to volume, both of which are extensive properties. On the other hand, mass itself is not an intensive property because it directly depends on the amount of material present. A classic example illustrating the distinction between intensive and extensive properties is the question, What weighs more, a pound of feathers or a pound of lead? While the weight (an extensive property) is the same, the density (an intensive property) differs significantly between the two materials. In thermodynamics, describing a system requires at least one intensive property and one extensive property. For example, if a set of parameters {a_i} represents intensive quantities and another set {A_j} represents extensive quantities, then a function F({a_i},{A_j}) is considered an intensive quantity if it remains unchanged when the system is scaled. A practical example of this is density, which is calculated as the ratio of mass (extensive) to volume (extensive), resulting in an intensive property. When two systems or substances are combined, the resulting value of an intensive property is typically a weighted mean of the individual values, provided there is no interaction between the substances. For instance, if two substances, A and B, with respective masses (m_A) and (m_B), and densities (V_A) and (V_B), are combined, the resulting density of the mixture can be calculated as a weighted average. For example, combining 60 kg of lead (density 11.34 g/cm³) with 40 kg of tin (density 6.99 g/cm³) results in a 100 kg mixture with a density of 9.60 g/cm³. This principle also applies to other intensive properties, such as temperature in a mixture of two ideal gases, where the final temperature is a weighted mean based on the number of particles and their respective temperatures. These properties are intrinsic to the material and do not depend on the system's size. In contrast, an extensive quantity, also known as an extensive variable or parameter, is a physical quantity that is proportional to the size of the system it describes. Extensive properties can be summed across subsystems to describe the entire system. For example, the total mass of a system is the sum of the masses of its individual components. Dividing one extensive property by another often yields an intensive property, such as dividing mass by volume to calculate density. Extensive quantities are homogeneous functions of degree 1 with respect to the system's size. This means that if the system's size is scaled by a factor, the extensive property will scale by the same factor. Examples of extensive properties include mass, length, volume, entropy, enthalpy, energy, electrical resistance, texture, and heat. It is important to distinguish physical properties from perceptions, as perceptions are fundamentally different. Perceptions, such as color or loudness, are subjective and depend on the observer's response. For example, the color of a potassium permanganate solution may appear pink, purple, or black depending on its concentration and the optical path length. While the optical absorption spectrum of the solution is a measurable physical property, the perceived color is not. For instance, the temperature of an object is an intensive physical property, and all observers will agree on which object is hotter. Similarly, the hue of a solution is related to the position of its spectral absorption maxima, but the perceived color may vary. In summary, while physical properties like temperature, density, and mass are measurable and objective, perceptions such as color and loudness are subjective and depend on the observer's interpretation.
